By providing a summary statistic about underlying household circumstances, it is plausible that access to an algorithmic tool could improve decision quality and child outcomes. 2.4 Model of Decisions with Algorithm Support We develop a theoretical model to clarify how an algorithm support tool could affect decision-making. Each child has an unobserved maltreatment risk r, assumed in the context of this model to follow a normal distribution.6 Assume for the purposes of this application that the mean and standard deviation of the normal distribution are such that r is almost always positive. In the absence of a CPS intervention, a child’s realized harm is entirely determined by risk r. CPS workers can address this risk, however. Workers observe a noisy indicator of maltreatment risk, m = r + ε, where ε is a normal error term with mean zero that is independent from r. Workers are constrained by state legal requirements in how they are instructed to respond to certain allegations (Appendix B2), so the model’s objective function is to minimize errors in estimating maltreatment risk based on the signal workers receive (i.e., accuracy in discerning risk) rather than solely minimizing child harm. Whereas underestimating risk could harm children, overestimating risk is costly in terms of worker time and effort, agency resources, and increases the risk of litigation. Hence, workers’ objective is to accurately assess child maltreatment risk. As in Aigner and Cain (1977), workers estimate risk using an empirical Bayes estimator: E[r|m] = (1−γ)α +γm, (1) where α = E[r] is the mean risk in the population and γ is the reliability of the signal as a measure of true risk, defined as γ = V(r) V(r)+V(ε). Thus, in the absence of any information m, workers fully rely on the group mean to assess risk, and they rely increasingly on m as they become more confident in its signal-to-noise ratio. The value p = r −E[r|m] describes the extent to which workers misestimate a child’s true risk. When workers underestimate child risk, they do not intervene appropriately in the child’s family and the child is susceptible to harm. The harm that a child experiences is a function of workers’ prediction error, denoted 6The normal distribution provides closed-form solutions in contrast to alternative distributional assumptions. 11 as H(p). For simplicity, we assume a functional form of H(p) = p21(p ≥0). The function is convex to convey the fact that large underestimation of risk is particularly costly in terms of child harm. In this model, overestimating risk does not harm the child (H(p) = 0 when p ≤0), though it may be a misuse of resources. True maltreatment risk r is more comprehensive than only the algorithm’s prediction of foster care placement, which is based predominantly on child and family history. The algorithmic tool could still help workers ascertain a more accurate signal of risk, however. The information provided by the algorithm may reduce worker mistakes when checking families’ CPS history, prompt a better understanding of family circumstances, allow for more or better discussion of complementary information from the incoming alle- gation, help assess the allegation in relation to CPS history, or place greater focus on overarching household risk. Each of these potential mechanisms suggest that, in the context of this model, providing an algorithmic tool would reduce the noise in the risk assessment made by workers. PROPOSITION 1: Accuracy of Risk Assessment. If providing algorithmic information reduces noise in workers’ risk assessment (V(ε) ↓), then: 1. The accuracy of risk assessment with the algorithmic tool will improve: V(p) ↓. 2. Accuracy will improve more for groups with larger variance in true risk r. PROOF: See Appendix D. Proposition 1 indicates that if the algorithm helps reduce noise in workers’ risk assessment, then the distribution of workers’ prediction mistakes will be more compressed, especially in groups whose members have very different levels of risk. The intuition for this result is straightforward: workers will rely less on mean risk α because the signal m they receive is more valuable, and therefore workers’ expected mal- treatment risk will be closer to a child’s true maltreatment risk. A larger variance in true risk implies that the mean will be a worse predictor, and therefore benefits should be larger in groups with greater variance in true risk. Improvements in risk assessment subsequently affect child health as presented in the second proposition, which is analogous to the first proposition but for child harm. PROPOSITION 2: Reductions in Child Harm. If providing algorithmic information reduces noise in workers’ risk assessment (V(ε) ↓), then: 1. Child harm will decrease when workers have access to the algorithmic tool: E[H (p)] ↓. 2. Benefits from algorithmic tool use will be larger for groups with more variance in true risk r. PROOF: See Appendix D. 12 Note that until now, all of the above results assume that workers make correct assessments of mean risk: α = E[r]. One might be interested in relaxing this assumption, for example if workers overestimate risk for certain demographic groups. Disparities in risk estimation is a particularly relevant extension of the model given recent evidence that Child Protective Service workers may overestimate Black children’s risk, or underestimate white children’s risk (Baron et al., 2023). Proposition 3 takes this into account. PROPOSITION 3: Correcting Group-Level Differences in Estimated Risk. If workers overestimate the risk faced by children in given group B (αB > E[r|B]), then providing access to the algorithmic tool will reduce the size of prediction mistakes for those in group B, especially for children with a signal m far from αB. PROOF: See Appendix D. This final proposition indicates that when workers overestimate risk for certain subgroups, then provid- ing the algorithmic tool should decrease this overestimation of risk. Child harm may still fall on average for the group, if for example members of the group with overestimated risk were not concentrated in a part of the risk distribution where children were at risk of being harmed (r sufficiently low). 3 Data, Sample Characteristics, and Experimental Design 3.1 Data Sources The trial county maintains an extensive administrative data system, which we integrated with statewide hospitalization records and a tool randomization database. Implementation partners at the Centre for Social Data Analytics (CSDA) shared algorithm risk scores for all incoming referrals, as well as the randomized treatment status of households. The county’s child welfare integrated data system includes individual-specific identifiers that follow each person, child and adult, on each referral over time. The integrated data system includes detailed information about the referral (e.g., allegations and reporter), response to a referral, investigator safety and risk reports upon visiting the home, case openings, foster care placements, authorized services, court proceedings, relationships of persons to one another on a referral, and individual demographic information when known. Demographic characteristics of social workers involved with the referral are unavailable. Text data of hotline transcriptions of the allegation are unavailable. However, we have access to some de- identified text data from team discussion notes, recorded when teams were deciding whether to investigate 13 a family. Statewide hospital inpatient and emergency room (ER) records are maintained by the state’s hospital association. We partnered with the hospital association to integrate linked hospitalization records for all children in the sample as a way to measure ground truth outcomes with respect to health care utilization and maltreatment. Hospitalization data span from January 2020 through June 2022. Records were matched probabilistically using person-level identifiers (full name, date of birth, and gender) and include fields for: dates of admission and discharge, point of origin, facility type, admission priority, charged amount, diag- nosis codes, and procedure codes. Match probabilities were 95 percent or greater for nearly all children. Notably, children were matched to all hospitalizations in the state – not just hospitalizations in the trial county – to address concerns about differential migration. 86 percent of matched hospitalizations occurred within the trial county, and 93 percent occurred within either the trial county or a neighboring county. 3.2 Sample Characteristics The trial ran for 17 months from November 1, 2020 to March 29, 2022. During the trial, 4,681 unique chil- dren, appearing on 2,832 referrals, were successfully randomized into either having the algorithm available for social workers or not. Results are robust to controls for seasonality. 8Our comparisons use statistics from the 2023 U.S. Census Bureau and https://www.acf.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ cb/cm2022.pdf. 16 3.3 Experimental Design We designed a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to estimate the causal effect of providing algorithmic risk predictions on CPS worker decisions and child outcomes. Access to the algorithm was randomized at the household level, as the decision of whether to investigate a household is common to all children in the home. The first time a household was seen during the trial, it was randomized into either the intervention group or control group. Workflow was identical in the intervention and control groups except for the availability of the algorithm score (Appendix Figure A.5). For each referral, a social worker would look up the referral ID in the machine learning tool interface, read back the scores to the group, and the group note keeper would typically record scores in the discussion notes. When a family was in the intervention arm of the trial, the scores of all children in the household were shown (usually highly correlated), with the maximum being emphasized. When the family was in the control arm of the trial, the interface did not show any of the scores and workers would continue their standard discussion of the referral. Workers were aware of the trial and that the score would be (un)available for certain families at random. One novel contribution of our study design is that randomization was instantiated at the household level, such that re-referred children retained their original intervention or control status. This is a key difference from Fitzpatrick et al. (2022), where randomization was conducted at the day-team level such that re-referred families were re-randomized. Many children are called in multiple times per year, with the average child in our sample being referred slightly more than twice from November 2020 through July 2022 (Table 1). Our trial design allows us to estimate the medium-run effects of tool availability by ensuring that the control group would not have a score shown during the trial period. In the absence of contamination bias (i.e., spillovers from treatment to control; discussed in Section 4.1), our estimated effects compare a world where the tool is consistently available to a counterfactual world without any access to algorithmic information. Ensuring that households kept their original intervention status was difficult in a setting where house- holds are often non-nuclear in structure. Multiple families living in the same household and unstable parental relationships are more common among CPS-involved families. Our solution randomized mothers to either intervention or control, and then assigned children to their biological mother’s intervention status. Due to an unintentional coding error from the implementing partner, a small subset of observations were randomized only conditional on family size, leading us to include corrective “randomization controls” in our preferred specification. This minor correction for partial conditional randomization is described in Appendix C. 17 3.4 Empirical Strategy The empirical strategy in this paper estimates the effect of having an algorithm tool available. For child i first scored on referral r(i), we estimate: (2) Yi = δ0 + δ1AlgoAccessr(i) + γs(i) + εi where Yi is the outcome of interest pertaining to child i on referral r(i). AlgoAccessr(i) is a binary {0,1} intervention status indicator, equal to one if the algorithm tool was available to the team during their dis- cussion of the child’s first referral r(i) during the trial, and zero if the algorithm was not available. γs(i) are randomization procedure controls for sibling group size for referrals without a recorded mother after March 2021, which address a minor implementation glitch (see Appendix C for more details). Finally, εi is an error term representing additional, unexplained variation in the outcome. Standard errors are clustered conservatively at the household (overlapping family network) level.9 Equation 2 estimates the level effect of tool availability, δ1, on outcome Yi. Under conditional random assignment of tool availability, such that E[εi|AlgoAccessr(i),γs(i)] = 0, the estimate ˆδ1 can be interpreted as the causal effect of access to the algorithm on a child’s outcome of interest. Validation of Algorithm Use and Random Assignment The effectiveness of algorithmic decision aids depends on if and when workers choose to use them, which is in part a function of human trust in algorithm tools (see Glikson and Woolley, 2020, for a review). Since workers were strongly encouraged but not required to consult the tool in our setting, the policy-relevant treatment effect is the intent-to-treat (ITT) effect of giving workers access to the algorithm. Using de-identified discussion notes, we ascertain that workers wrote down algorithm scores in at least 73 percent of instances when available in our sample (Table A.2). This fraction of observed and recorded scores is relatively constant across the algorithm risk score distribution (Table A.2, column 2). The recorded share is likely an underestimate of the true rate of algorithm consultation: workers may have consulted the tool but forgotten to write down the score in their meeting notes. Our findings show that workers regularly chose to consult the algorithm, even though its use was not monitored by leadership and there were no professional repercussions for not using it. 9A household cluster is defined conservatively as any network of individuals who share a connected path with one another, as measured by common appearances on a referral. In practice, there is no difference from clustering at the referral level (Appendix Table A.6). 18 Random assignment of the intervention is important for estimating unbiased causal effects of algorithm availability on outcomes. We check for evidence of random assignment by running a balance test, regressing assignment status on a vector of salient pre-randomization observable characteristics. Table A.3 suggests that the algorithm was randomized successfully: we do not find joint significance of the coefficients on observable characteristics. The p-value of the F-test is 0.438 in the full sample, and 0.106 in the hospital sample. To address potential concerns regarding the lower p-value in the hospital outcomes sample, we conduct a robustness test in Appendix Table A.6 that controls for all the variables from these balance tests in our main specifications. 4 Results Despite Child Protective Service’s primary objective of protecting children, few studies have produced causal estimates of the impact of CPS policies on child injury and other health outcomes. We link statewide hospitalization records from the trial state’s hospital association (Section 3.1) to measure the effect of algo- rithmic information on ground-truth outcomes. This section covers three main findings: a reduction in child harm, a reduction in child harm disparities, and a reduction in racial CPS surveillance disparities. We document the mechanisms behind these results in the subsequent section on mechanisms (Section 5). In particular, as context for the current section, the algorithm did not change the average rate of CPS intervention, but helped improve workers’ allocation of interventions. 4.1 Impact of Algorithm Availability on Child Health and Wellbeing We estimate the impact of worker access to the algorithm on child wellbeing. Our preferred outcome is an aggregated “harm index” of pre-specified hospitalization outcomes. The pre-analysis plan included sev- eral outcomes that we expected to be associated with child maltreatment: a child’s number of high-priority hospital visits (emergency, urgent, or trauma-related), visits with injury ICD codes, preventable emergency room visits (potential proxy for neglect), injury ICD codes for intentional harm (assault, self-harm), and ICD codes for maltreatment, which are rare. “Preventable ER visits” are the number of child admissions for ambulatory care sensitive conditions (ACSC, defined using Appendix 8 of Carey et al. 2017), for example an ER visit for asthma which could have been avoided had the child received proper preventative treatment 19 and supervision. We then aggregate all outcomes into a combined harm index. The index is the standardized average of the five variables described above, each standardized. Variables are standardized (mean 0, vari- ance 1) using the control sample, and a lower value of the harm index is considered better for the child. In Appendix Table A.6 we also consider an alternative harm index which uses only a binary, extensive margin for all five outcome categories (e.g., any high-priority, any injury, etc.), as well as several other ways of ag- gregating these outcomes together. Point estimates are negative across all five outcomes, suggesting that providing access to the algorithm improved outcomes on all five dimensions. Furthermore, the point estimates are large relative to the means in the control group. In particular, the algorithmic tool reduced the average number of future injury admissions by 29 percent, or 0.06 admissions relative to a mean of 0.21 (p < 0.05). In the second-to-last row at the bottom of the table, we test whether we can reject that the tool caused harm for any listed outcome, on average. The p-values of these one-sided tests allow us to confidently rule out an increase in harm for at least three of the five outcomes reported in columns 2-6. Accumulated harm for this top percent ranged from 2.6 to 29 standard deviations above the mean, with the median child in this group having a high priority hospital visit every three months. Appendix Figure A.6 provides a visualization of the change in distribution of the harm index with the tool. Relatedly, as shown in Appendix Figure A.7, benefits of the algorithm appear to be greatest for children with the highest algorithm-predicted risk scores (top quintile) who may be at greatest risk of maltreatment (control group levels of harm in Appendix Figure A.7). The majority of children with an explicit maltreatment-related hospital ICD code had a harm index in the top one percent of the harm distribution, which suggests that the algorithm may have reduced child maltreatment. The reduction in child harm does not appear to be driven by changes in willingness to seek care. One potential concern is that tool access could reduce children’s hospital visits for reasons other than child harm, such as fear of being re-reported to CPS. To distinguish changes in welfare from changes in care-seeking, we report placebo tests of outcomes that are not thought to be associated with child maltreatment: child cancer-related hospitalizations (following Vaithianathan et al. 2020) and COVID-related hospitalizations. These estimates are reported in columns 1 and 2 of Appendix Table A.4. Access to the algorithm had no 21 impact on either placebo outcome, nor on lower-priority hospital visits that are less likely to indicate severe maltreatment. Tool access did not significantly reduce the overall incidence or frequency of hospital inter- actions (Columns 3 and 4 of Appendix Table A.4). Therefore, providing the algorithmic tool significantly decreased the number of hospitalizations associated with maltreatment, but not the total number of hospital interactions. The benefits of the algorithm must be weighed against its implementation and development costs. To do so, we must make assumptions regarding (i) the number of instances of maltreatment that were prevented by accessing to the algorithm tool and (ii) the cost of maltreatment. Assume for simplicity that when CPS reduces the likelihood of a child placing in the top one percent of the harm index, it is because CPS in- tervention prevented child maltreatment. Access to the algorithmic tool reduced the number of children at the top of the harm distribution by approximately n = 20 relative to the control group (Table 2, Column 7), implying about 20 fewer victims of maltreatment. The lower bound of the estimated lifetime costs of mal- treatment in the literature is $250,000 (in 2020 USD) per affected child, with about a fourth of this amount attributable to government expenditures in special education, criminal justice, and public health insurance (Fang et al., 2012). We multiply the total maltreatment cost by the number of beneficiaries to calculate a back-of-the-envelope estimate of $5.0M lifetime benefits from the algorithm in the trial sample, not count- ing the psychological benefits of reduced exposure to maltreatment. The initial fixed cost of developing the tool was $250k, with an additional $15k in annual maintenance costs.11 Given that implementation costs (about $280k over two years) are much smaller than estimated public savings from reduced maltreatment (20· $250k 4 = $1.25M), our estimates suggest an infinite marginal value of public funds (MVPF) of the algo- rithmic tool. The estimates also imply that the benefits within the trial sample alone outweigh the one-time costs of designing the tool, which has the potential to scale to other agencies. Additional benefits of the algorithm, such as reduced group-specific disparities in hospitalization and surveillance (subsections 4.2 and 4.3), are not included in the cost-benefit calculation. Furthermore, the tool did not significantly affect the amount of time spent making a decision: we estimate a small, imprecise reduction in discussion time (Figure A.11).12 These back-of-the-envelope estimates are consistent with recent scholarship showing that algorithmic decision aids exhibit high social returns across a variety of domains (Ludwig et al., 2024). 11This information was provided by Rhema Vaithianathan and the Centre for Social Data Analytics. 12Other studies have found time-saving benefits of algorithmic tools (Agarwal et al., 2023; Noy and Zhang, 2023), but a lack of significant changes in discussion time may not be surprising in this context. Workers still must consult family history to understand the context behind a referral, and the discussion of family history is typically only a short part of the team discussion. Much of the discussion time is spent on the current allegation. 22 Changes in other policy-relevant outcomes are broadly consistent with a reduction in child harm from access to the algorithm. First, for the subset of children under age 10, there is a set of ICD codes that practitioners have identified as suggestive of maltreatment (Schnitzer et al. 2011). Point estimates suggest that providing the algorithm may have reduced the incidence of practitioner-defined maltreatment visits by about 36 percent, though estimates are imprecise due to restricting the sample to children under age 10, and because of the relative rarity of hospitalizations with practitioner-identified codes (Appendix Table A.4, column 6). Second, we examine the impact of the tool on child re-referrals and removals in Appendix Table A.5. Point estimates suggest that providing the algorithm reduced children’s re-referrals to CPS (-5 percent), but estimates are again not statistically significantly different from zero. We find no evidence of a reduction in child removals from the home, but this could be because removals are one of the means by which CPS attempts to prevent child maltreatment. We show in Section 5.1 that the algorithm helped workers target investigations to children at greater risk of harm, who could have benefited more from a removal. Finally, we find suggestive evidence of a five percent reduction in medical charges to public payer insurance for children with the algorithm, though these effects are not statistically significant (Appendix Table A.4, columns 7-8). We present a series of robustness tests for the main effects of the algorithm on child harm in Appendix Table A.6. The findings are robust to: a permutation test (p = 0.04), to controlling for all baseline character- istics, to excluding the first sixty days after a referral when children could get health examinations as a result of a CPS investigation, to including all days after a referral, and to including children referred after October 2021, for whom we have only a few months of hospital data available after the referral. The findings are also robust to other ways of combining outcomes into a harm index, such as using a weighted index, using an index with only outcomes’ extensive margins, and using a first principal component. Finally, results are robust to alternative clustering of standard errors and to a bounding exercise for treatment non-compliance.13 Importantly, tool access did not crowd out resources provided to children in the control group. Table A.7 tests for the presence of short-run, within-day spillovers (i.e., contamination) by leveraging the share of referrals that were treated during the day, excluding a child’s own referral. If benefits had come at the expense of the control group, then, assuming fixed resources per day, one might expect to see: (1) worse outcomes for children in the control group as the percent treated in the day increases, and possibly also (2) weaker effects for treated children as the percent of children treated in the day increases. We find no 13As discussed in Appendix C, n = 61 children in the hospital sample control group had the algorithmic tool available due to changes in family structure. 23 evidence of spillover effects in terms of screen-ins, discussion time, or child harm. Children for whom the tool was available benefited without imposing costs on other children. Our specification may underestimate the benefits of the algorithm if workers were to learn from using the tool. In this scenario, we would expect indirect benefits for children in the control group, and an attenuation of treatment effects over time. Splitting children into three equally-sized groups by referral date, we find no evidence suggesting that workers learned from the algorithmic tool over the course of the trial (Figure A.8). To the extent that there was unobserved learning by workers, our study estimates would likely be a conservative lower bound on the true impacts of providing the algorithm. 4.2 Impact of Algorithm Availability on Group Disparities in Health and Wellbeing A significant concern about algorithmic decision aids is their potential to perpetuate and widen inequal- ity. On the one hand, algorithms trained on past history could embed human bias and potentially amplify oversurveillance and/or underservice of children from certain disadvantaged backgrounds (Obermeyer et al. 2019). Additionally, machine learning predictions can sometimes be more accurate for large majority groups, and be less effective or even detrimental for members of minority groups (Larrazabal et al., 2020). From a policy perspective, these concerns have contributed to either the disadoption or critical coverage of similar algorithmic decision supports in Oregon and Pennsylvania.14 On the other hand, given widespread complaints about systemic bias in criminal justice and social service contexts, algorithms may be less biased than the status quo of human decision-makers (c.f., Hoffman et al. 2018, Kleinberg et al. 2018, Arnold et al. 2024), or may even reverse bias depending on selection into the training data (Rambachan and Roth, 2020). Machine learning can also detect and respond to disparities often unknown to human experts (Pierson et al. 2021) or cause people to think about information more deliberatively in a manner that reduces subconscious bias (Agan et al. 2022). Ultimately, the impact that algorithm plus human decision systems have on disparities depends on how humans choose to use – or misuse – algorithmic information. Past evidence suggests that human users may override recommendations in ways that can either amplify or reduce disparities (Albright 2023; Cheng et al. 2022). Given theoretical ambiguity on the impacts of algorithmic decision supports on disparities, it is important to gather empirical evidence. We report effects of algorithm availability on disparities in health by race, gender, ethnicity, and socioe- 14https://www.npr.org/2022/06/02/1102661376/oregon-drops-artificial-intelligence-child-abuse-cases 24 conomic status (Figure 1 and Table A.8). When the tool was not available, as shown in light blue on the left side of each panel of Figure 1, children’s harm index is higher for Black children, Hispanic children, girls, and children from low-income families as measured by SNAP (food stamp) receipt. Table A.8 (row “Type”) formalizes this result: in the control group, differences between the specified group and out-group are statistically significant for girls, Hispanic children, and low-income children, and large but imprecise for Black children. Access to the algorithm significantly reduced harm for Black, Hispanic, female, and low-income chil- 25 dren (comparing light blue triangles to dark blue triangles in Figure 1). The out-groups (square dots) also experienced improvements in outcomes, but they were smaller in magnitude. Precise estimates are reported in Table A.8, and imply a reduction in disparities in the harm index on the order of 50 to 80 percent (Ta- ble A.8, bottom row). Although none of the reductions in disparities is statistically significant on its own, the cumulative evidence for a reduction in disparities is strong: we can confidently reject that none of the disparities change (p < 0.001, Table A.8). These findings are consistent with the theoretical model’s prediction that the algorithmic tool will lead to greater reductions in harm for groups with more variance in child risk (Proposition 2.2). Children who are Black, Hispanic, female, and from low-income families tend to face higher risk of child mortality (Currie and Schwandt, 2016) and/or maltreatment (Putnam-Hornstein et al., 2021). According to both our theoretical model and empirical findings, the benefits of providing the algorithm are more pronounced for children from these historically disadvantaged backgrounds. 4.3 Impact of Algorithm Availability on Racial Disparities in CPS Screen-Ins Providing algorithmic information may affect disparities in agency surveillance. CPS investigations can sometimes be intrusive and traumatic, and prior work has documented substantial racial disparities – in some cases unwarranted – in CPS contact across the U.S. (Kim et al. 2017, Edwards et al. 2021, Baron et al. 2023). In our sample, Black children are nearly twice as likely to be investigated as other children, even after conditioning on algorithm risk score (Table A.9). In contrast, we find no evidence of screen-in disparities by gender, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status even after controlling for algorithm-predicted risk (Table A.9). We therefore focus our analysis of surveillance disparities on race, specifically Black children relative to children who are not Black (primarily white). Figure 2 shows that, in the control group, Black children at below-median predicted risk were 60 per- centage points more likely to be screened in than other (primarily white) children of similar risk level. However, when the algorithm was available, below-median-risk Black children were screened in at much lower rates, comparable to rates for other children. These findings suggest that access to the algorithmic tool reduced unwarranted racial disproportionality in investigations among low-risk children. Although the trial county has a relatively small Black population, there were still n = 170 Black children in the full sample when using CPS-derived race alone, with at least 23 children in each race-by-treatment-status cell. Regres- sion estimates presented in column 1 of Appendix Table A.10 confirm a reduction in screen-ins for low-risk 26 Black children. Our theoretical model implies that workers will overestimate risk less when they have access to the algo- rithm because they can rely more on the signal of risk they receive instead of group means (Proposition 3). Our findings are consistent with this hypothesis. The considerable magnitude of the reduction in screen-in racial disparities among low-risk-score children, however, suggests that providing the algorithmic tool might additionally alter group stereotypes that workers use to make assessments. This is in line with theoretical work by Bordalo et al. (2016) on how stereotypes form from a representative agent. For low-scoring Black children, workers may have been prompted by the algorithm to change their reference means to that of other low-risk-score children: workers might use a different α in model equation 1 for low- and high-scoring Black children, respectively. Appendix Table A.10 shows that reductions in surveillance disparities from the tool are reasonably ro- bust under a variety of tests and design decisions: a permutation test, excluding Hispanic children, excluding children with missing race, recoding children with missing race as white or Black, using a combination of CPS-reported and hospital-reported race, and using algorithm score level (1-20) instead of a binary measure of above versus below median score. Although the exact magnitude, and corresponding power to detect significant effects, of the disparity in screen-in rates for below-median-risk children depends on the speci- fication, providing the algorithm consistently reduces surveillance disparities conditional on risk or, taking the imprecise point estimates at face value, cancels them out entirely. 27 Black children are nearly twice as likely have an above-median algorithm risk score relative to the rest of the sample. We therefore examine the impact of providing the algorithm on racial disparities in absolute terms; in other words, not conditioning on predicted risk. Column 2 of Appendix Table A.10 shows that the algorithm tool reduced screen-ins by 13 percentage points for Black children across the sample, driven by the sharp reduction in screen-ins for low-risk Black children. Tool availability approximately halved unconditional racial disparities in screen-ins, though the point estimate is not statistically significant due to a relatively modest number of Black children in the sample. Finally, the reduction in screen-ins for below-median-risk-score Black children came with no clear ad- verse consequences for measured child harm. We are underpowered to exclude an increase in child harm, but levels of the harm index among low-scoring Black children were similar regardless of tool availability (Appendix Figure A.10i). Reduced racial disparities in surveillance may be a function of humans and algorithms working together: a combination of both the information revealed by the algorithm and the training that workers receive. Social workers in the study county were trained in cultural competency with an eye toward fair treatment of families, and sensitivity toward equitable treatment by race, ethnicity, sexual orientation, and language. From our discussions with social workers after the trial, we think it is possible that receiving a low algorithm score provided workers with the confidence to screen out a child that may have otherwise been investigated due to a tethering of the worker’s belief of potential maltreatment to the group mean (model proposition 3, Section 2.4). While this analysis provides a valuable example of human-algorithm complementarity, future work will need to explore the circumstances under which such a reduction in disparities translates to other settings with different family demographics and where workers may differ in beliefs or training. We revisit the analysis in Section 6.3, where we consider the equity advantage of human-plus-algorithm decisions compared to a counterfactual algorithm-only decision rule. 5 Mechanisms Giving workers access to an algorithm that predicts child risk improved child outcomes and reduced racial disparities. Our theoretical model attributes these benefits to improvements in workers’ assessments of child risk (Proposition 1). In this section, we provide evidence of improved worker decision-making and rule out a number of alternative mechanisms. 28 5.1 Algorithm Improves Worker Allocation of Screen-Ins The intervention did not increase the total number of investigations (“screen-ins”) or any other measurable level of services (Figure A.11). Workers did not increase overall levels of intervention, nor did they provide greater levels of one intervention in place of another, as is sometimes observed due to asymmetric valuation of false positives and false negatives (Almog et al. 2024, Fitzpatrick et al. 2022). In our setting, levels of intervention may be relatively inelastic given legal, financial, and time constraints. Although targeting of screen-ins could theoretically improve without significant effects on any of these three margins (targeting to children at higher risk that is unobservable on those dimensions, for instance children not yet bearing injuries, children not recently hospitalized, and mar- 31 gins of future harm that our simple prediction model does not capture), these findings bolster the evidence that algorithmic information improved CPS allocation of screen-ins. It may seem surprising that workers better allocated investigations based on potential child harm, despite not increasing investigations for children with high algorithm risk scores. These facts permit a number of hypotheses, and rule out others (Table A.11). The hypothesis most consistent with our findings is that workers leverage expertise that is complementary to the algorithmic tool, as will be explored in greater detail in Section 5.3. Reminiscent of Bhatt et al. (2024), social workers in our setting may allocate screen- ins based partly on expected treatment effects (proverbially ˆβ) rather than expected outcome levels (ˆy). In other words, not all children with high algorithm scores will necessarily benefit from CPS investigation, and vice versa. Finally, the magnitudes for the improvement in screen-in targeting reported in columns 1 and 4 of Table 3 (approximately 0.1 SD) are large enough to potentially explain the entire reduction in child harm with algorithm support (-0.06 SD). Enhanced targeting of screen-ins could have also led to better targeting of subsequent CPS actions, though we are underpowered to examine this. Targeting of other concurrent in- terventions (e.g., law enforcement, community services) could also have improved, but screen-ins are the primary margin of CPS attention. In either event, child outcomes improved with algorithm support because workers made better assessments of child risk, as evidenced by better screening decisions. We provide additional evidence of this in Section 5.2. 5.2 Improvements in Targeting Reduce Child Harm and Harm Disparities Certain disadvantaged groups have historically had greater variance in mortality and child maltreatment risk (Currie and Schwandt, 2016; Putnam-Hornstein et al., 2021). Our model predicts greater improvements in the accuracy of workers’ perceptions of risk for members of these groups, which in turn should lead to greater reductions in harm relative to others (Propositions 1.2 and 2.2). Consistent with our model, we find that children in demographic groups that experienced the greatest targeting improvements with the algorithm also experienced the greatest reductions in measured harm (Fig- ure 4). These findings more broadly suggest that reductions in harm are attributable at least in part to improvements in targeting of screen-ins. In this section we provide suggestive evidence of how access to algorithmic information changed workers’ decision-making process. To do so, we leverage rich, unstructured administrative text data from the partnered child welfare agency, taken from discussion notes written during workers’ decision-making process. Table B1 contains examples of subsets of these conversa- tions and subsequent team decisions. We analyzed text data using our theory of change for how the algorithm could affect decision-making (Section 2.4).17 The algorithmic tool was based on data from household members’ past history and reported a score for each child listed on the call. (2022) view cognitive load as a critical determinant of whether algorithmic tools are com- plementary to human expertise. Complicated interfaces or unnecessary alerts from algorithmic decision supports could contribute to cognitive overload. In contrast, a machine learning tool designed in collabo- ration with users could reduce what cognitive theory calls extraneous (modifiable) cognitive load (Sweller, 2011). In our setting, having an algorithm aggregate vast, disorganized historical data could allow workers to reallocate effort to other inherently difficult parts of their decision task (intrinsic cognitive load). According to cognitive load theory, one would expect greater improvements in welfare when cases are complex and where workers are more likely to benefit from algorithm support in making family history more digestible. In Table 4, we consider heterogeneity in algorithm benefits under three distinct indicators of complexity: (1) discussion notes that mention uncertainty about a child’s situation or how to address it, containing expressions such as “?”, “unknown”, “unclear”, and “uncertain” (column 1), (2) decisions that take longer than 15 minutes, corresponding to the top quartile of decision length (column 2), and (3) children with a recent prior potential-maltreatment-related hospitalization (column 3). Each of the three measures captures a distinct dimension of complexity: the largest correlation coefficient between any two complexity measures is ρ = 0.16. Algorithm support did not affect the frequency of uncertainty-related text markers nor the probability of a long discussion, either in levels or when interacted by score, and the third proxy for complexity was exogenous to tool availability. Did the algorithmic tool’s informational content (risk score) matter, or did its presence merely serve as a behavioral reminder or nudge to workers? Although difficult to answer definitively, the fact that workers regularly checked and recorded the algorithm score – or lack thereof – in both the intervention and control groups (Appendix Figure A.5), together with score-based heterogeneity in discussion content and decisions (Figures 2 and 5) suggest that benefits of the algorithm are tied to the process of reviewing the predicted risk scores. Although the specific 1-to-20 value of the algorithm’s risk score likely helped workers allocate their attention more effectively, we cannot definitively rule out benefits from a general increase in the salience of family history – or other characteristics – upon seeing a listed score, regardless of its magnitude. An important topic for future research is understanding the impacts of the manner through which information is presented to users in similar settings. 6 Human-plus-Algorithm vs. Algorithm-Only Counterfactuals To what extent do human decision-makers contribute their independent expertise to improve upon algorith- mic predictions? As machine learning decision supports become more widespread, so do questions about 37 human experts’ contributions to decisions, and when to defer to machine decisions. In this study, outcomes improved when workers were given access to an algorithm. Workers, however, did not target investigations toward children with higher algorithm risk scores, but instead used complementary information more effec- tively. Given how well the algorithm risk score predicts meaningful outcomes (Appendix Figure A.3), it is reasonable to ask if outcomes could have improved even more if workers had based decisions more closely on the algorithm risk score. In this section, we conduct two innovative counterfactual exercises to estimate the impact of deferring to an algorithm to make decisions. We assess whether child harm and equity would have improved under (i) investigation decisions determined solely by algorithm predictions, and (ii) marginal increased reliance on algorithm predictions. This methodology can be applied in other experimental settings to assess whether users underutilize algorithmic information. Parts of the methodology can also be applied to study hypothet- ical, alternative decision rules beyond the implemented algorithm. 6.1 Counterfactual 1: Deferring Entirely to an Algorithm The first counterfactual exercise uses a bounding approach to estimate the impact of fully deferring screening decisions to the algorithm. The experiment did not include an algorithm-only treatment arm due to legal constraints: the statutory requirements for a screen-in do not always correspond to high algorithm-predicted risk. The algorithm provided a prediction of child risk, rather than a recommendation about whether to screen in the child. We suppose that algorithm recommendations would follow a simple decision rule where the al- gorithm screens in children with the highest predicted risk. The counterfactual exercise operates as follows: 1. Sort children by the algorithm’s predicted risk score. 2. Holding screen-in rates constant with the other treatment arms at 30 percent, screen in the riskiest 30 percent of children as predicted by the algorithm. 3. Estimate child outcomes conditional on the new screening decisions. To estimate counterfactual outcomes under this algorithm-based decision rule, we classify children from the control group in a 2-by-2 grid defined by screen-in decisions made by humans (observed) and by hy- pothetical algorithm recommendations (inferred above with minimal assumptions). The four states are as 38 follows: Humans and algorithm each decide to screen in, humans and algorithm each screen out, humans screen in but the algorithm would screen out, and humans screened out but the algorithm would screen in. The grid is presented in Table A.13. We directly observe child health outcomes when both parties, humans and algorithm, agree on the screen-in decision (both screen in, or both screen out). Second, for children screened in by human decision-makers but for whom the algorithm would have screened out, we make an assumption in favor of the algorithm. We assume that child health would not have been any worse if these children had been screened out, allowing us to impute the counterfactual outcome using observed child harm. This gives a best-case bound of outcomes if screening decisions were deferred to the algorithm. Finally, we must estimate outcomes for children observed to be screened out by humans, but in the counterfactual screened in by the algorithm. We allow counterfactual outcomes for this cell to vary over a range of values for how much a screen-in reduces child harm, assuming homogeneous impacts of screen-in and a floor value for child harm. The counterfactual outcome for children screened out by humans and screened in by the algorithm is calculated as: max(yi −R,H), where yi is the realized outcome for child i, R is the hypothetical effect of a screen-in, and H is the minimum possible value of standardized child harm (zero visits for all hospitalization types included in the harm index). Though developed independently, this methodology shares similarities with Ben-Michael et al. (2024) who also propose a bounding approach. Results of this counterfactual exercise are plotted in Figure 6. We compare child harm under a best case for our algorithm-only scenario (dashed orange line) with outcomes observed under human-only (dashed light blue line) and human-plus-algorithm decision-making (solid blue line with confidence band). The algorithm-only counterfactual outperforms the human-only scenario by construction, because it was as- sumed that children screened in by humans but screened out by the algorithm were not harmed by the screen out. This assumption is visualized by the algorithm-only line falling below the human-only line. The hor- izontal axis varies the effect of a screen-in for children that humans screened out but the algorithm would have screened in. These hypothetical screen-in effects range from zero to four standard-deviation reductions in harm. The vertical axis shows the average child harm index across the sample, for each hypothetical effect of a screen-in. We expect the actual treatment effect of a screen-in to be toward the far left of the axis (< 1 SD reduction in harm), given that a screen-in is not a panacea, and given that the gap in harm between the most severely maltreated children (those in foster care) and the remainder of the sample is less than 0.5 standard deviations. Therefore, under reasonable assumptions that favor the algorithm, we find that child outcomes under a human-plus-algorithm scenario are better than, though statistically indistinguishable 39 from, the algorithm-only best-case rule under realistic screen-in treatment effects (< 1 SD), and similar un- der larger treatment effects. This result highlights the limits to fully automating complex social decisions with an algorithm, and provides evidence in favor of human-algorithm complementarity in our setting. The algorithm used only historical data, whereas social workers had access to both historical data and real-time, detailed caller reports about why a family was being referred. Since the algorithm was designed to complement human decision-making, a relevant coun- terfactual exercise is to evaluate a marginal increase in using the algorithm score to guide decisions, rather than fully deferring to the algorithm decision rule. Increased marginal reliance corresponds to screening in additional children that the algorithm predicted as high risk. A real-life analog of this would be a manda- tory screen-in protocol for families scoring above a high-risk threshold, similar to what was implemented in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (Lacey et al., 2024). We find that potential benefits from deferring more to an algorithm have already been realized by stan- dard human oversight over algorithm predictions. Figure 7 shows realized child harm for children not investigated by CPS, by treatment status and algorithm-predicted risk level. Each point represents the mean harm index of screened-out children with a given algorithm risk score. Among these children, an algorithm- only decision-maker would first prioritize screening in those with the highest risk scores, on the right side of the figure. We first note a striking opportunity for potential welfare improvements under algorithmic decision support: when the tool was not available, children with a score of 20 who were not investigated experienced harm levels almost 0.6 SD above the mean (light blue line with circles). Social workers were missing out on a subset of high-scoring children in the control group who accrued significant harm, such that a mandatory screen-in protocol for these children might have readily improved outcomes. In contrast, 41 worker access to algorithmic information (dark blue line with diamonds) improved screen-in targeting and greatly attenuated any potential benefits from mandating screen-ins for top risk scores, despite the fact that screen-out rates remained unchanged at the top of the score distribution. With algorithm access, the reduc- tion in harm for screened-out children on referrals scoring a 20 is statistically significant at the 10 percent level (β = −0.44, p = 0.071). For high algorithm risk scores, the mean harm for screened-out children un- der algorithm availability is approximately 0 to 0.1 SD greater than the control group mean. In other words, most of the capacity for harm reduction is already realized by social workers using the algorithm freely, such that further gains from a screen-in mandate would be comparatively modest, especially relative to the costs of additional investigations that would result from such a policy. Requiring a mandatory screen-in for all children with an algorithm score of 20 would result in a sizable 20 percent (6 percentage point) increase in overall screen-in rates.18 Figure 7 therefore highlights two key points about human-plus-algorithm gains. First, the algorithm helped workers target investigations more effectively. Although workers did not change their screen-in rates for children with the highest algorithm risk scores when using the tool (Figure 3), workers did screen in a set of ex-post more vulnerable children. Second, workers used complementary information not available to the algorithm to reduce harm. In situations where workers “disagreed” with the algorithm (high algorithm score, worker screen-out), child outcomes were not substantially worse than those for other screened-out children in the sample. Therefore, ex-post partial automation of investigation decisions using algorithm predictions alone is likely to be of limited benefit in our setting. Future work with larger study samples could consider partial automation with optimal triage, as proposed by Raghu et al. This can be done using the initial counterfactual exercise described in Section 6.1. The algorithm-only counterfactual for screen-in disparities is nearly assumption-free because hypothetical screen-in recommendations can be di- rectly deduced from ordering algorithm risk scores from high to low (Section 6.1). We do not need to make any assumptions about how a screen-in impacts child harm. Figure 8 shows CPS surveillance (screen-in) disparities for relevant demographic subgroups under three decision regimes: human-only, human-plus- algorithm, and algorithm-only. We find that human-plus-algorithm decisions improved equity not only compared to the status quo of human experts alone, but also compared to counterfactual screen-ins from the algorithm without human oversight. Relative to an algorithm-only decision rule, human oversight reduced disparities in CPS inves- tigations by race, ethnicity, gender, and socioeconomic status: the dark blue squares in Figure 8 (human 43 with algorithm) are always closer to zero than the orange diamonds (algorithm only), though point estimates are in some cases imprecise. Second, the algorithm on its own would have investigated significantly more Hispanic children and more low-income children relative to the status quo of human experts on their own (light blue triangles). This second finding is to some extent consistent with social workers’ concerns that algorithmic tools could perpetuate historical bias in CPS intervention (Stapleton et al., 2022). Notably, in- creased surveillance under the algorithm-only counterfactual does not correspond with a reduction in harm for these subgroups relative to observed human-plus-algorithm decision-making (Appendix Figure A.15), suggesting that the algorithm-only disparities may not be warranted. In short, the improvements in equity observed during the trial would not have been fully realized – and for some groups may have worsened – without human oversight of the algorithm. Providing algorithm support to humans leads to more equitable levels of surveillance by CPS, relative to the algorithm on its own. In certain settings, combining algorithm support with human expert oversight could be an effective strategy to overcome public skepticism about algorithms and the perpetuation of disparities. 7 Conclusion Machine learning tools have drawn increased interest and scrutiny in social service and criminal justice settings, including Child Protective Services (CPS). This paper offers one of the first randomized evaluations of human-algorithm interaction in such a context. CPS represents an important and generalizable use case for evaluating algorithmic decision supports. Like many public agencies, Child Protective Services (i) have long-accumulated histories of administrative data that are useful for predictive risk modeling, and (ii) require critical, time-sensitive decisions from workers with limited experience and high turnover. Our trial’s high- stakes field setting, reasonably representative sample of children referred to CPS during the study period, and the algorithm’s scaling potential given its implementation in other counties (in Colorado, Pennsylvania, and California), provides cautious optimism for external validity (c.f., List 2020). We find that humans and algorithms are complementary in our setting: both decision quality and equity improve compared to when humans or algorithms make decisions on their own. When humans had access to algorithm support, child injury-related hospitalizations fell by 29 percent and social workers prevented two thirds of extreme child harm (top percentile of child harm index). The algorithm was designed as an aid rather than a replacement for human workers, who were acutely aware of what information was included in the algorithm versus available exclusively to them. In this context, algorithm support helped workers parse through new, complementary information about families. The algorithm helped workers reduce their tendency to investigate Black children, particularly for those scored as low risk, and conversely human oversight helped reduce CPS surveillance that the algorithm would have otherwise induced for Hispanic and 45 low-income households. Human-algorithm complementarity is thus salient not just for efficiency but also for equity. Our model and documented mechanisms rationalize these findings and suggest they could appear in other decision environments when algorithms reduce the noise in the decision-making process, such as through prompting richer discussion of critical information or reducing extraneous cognitive load. In light of evidence from previous literature on benefits from group decision making (Galton, 1907; Simoiu et al., 2019; Chiang et al., 2023), the fact that the algorithm in our setting was given to a group of workers who needed to reach a consensus decision may have played a role in its effectiveness. Although the evaluation in this paper took place over multiple years, it is important that future work estimate the effects of algorithmic decision support over even longer time horizons. Algorithmic tools may affect workers’ competence, the pipeline of future decisions, and the types of workers that a firm can recruit or retain through algorithms’ effects on turnover (Brynjolfsson et al. 2023). Recent studies have articulated concerns about worker deskilling or turnover when algorithms replace expertise (Rinta-Kahila et al., 2018; Grennan and Michaely, 2020). However, in a complex social setting such as child protection where complementary worker expertise seems critical, long-run effects could be more consistent with emerging studies showing that humans can learn to make novel and better decisions over time when interacting with AI (Shin et al., 2023). Longer-run evaluations could yield further insights on how algorithms can be adapted, statistically or dynamically, to human cognitive biases (Kleinberg et al. 2024). Finally, although the use of predictive risk modeling is valuable for refining worker decisions, our dis- cussions with workers highlight limits to professional discretion. In our context, agencies are statutorily required to have supporting (non-algorithm) evidence to investigate a referral for alleged maltreatment, whereas other types of allegations require an investigation regardless of human perception of risk. A statutorily-optimal policy must therefore investigate at least a fraction of predicted low-risk reports, and cannot investigate all high-risk reports. Abstracting away from human oversight and accountability would infringe on legal requirements, highlighting the need for algorithm designers to consider the incentives and behaviors of human decision makers. Consequently, identifying which context-specific features of human-algorithm interaction lead to the greatest efficiency gains remains a valuable area for future research. Promising research directions include identifying optimal decision points for deploying new algorithms, op- timal triage of decisions to algorithm-only versus human-only or human-plus-algorithm tracks, improving the explainability and presentation of predictive information, and understanding the impact of algorithms on individual versus group decision making. 46 References Abadie, Alberto, Matthew M. We measure margins of CPS intervention, such as high-risk-track screen-ins, using child welfare administrative data. Additional margins of intended intervention, such as voluntary resources sent to screened-out families, are inferred from team discussion notes. Some interventions are unobserved: services paid for by Medicaid, for example, are not included in administrative data. In this section we present all deviations from the pre-analysis plan. 1. Randomization Implementation Complications. It was not possible for us to anticipate the chal- lenges we would have in implementing the randomization. There were two unforeseen implementa- tion challenges with respect to household randomization that required us to adapt our design. - Between November 2020-March 2021, a small group of randomization statuses was uninten- tionally overwritten by our implementing partner. To address this, we omit the N = 238 children for whom treatment assignment is unknown. (See Appendix Table A.1 for details regarding sample restrictions.) - In March 2021, the implementing partner attempted to correct the error, but in doing so inadver- tently changed the randomization procedure and introduced two complications. First, when a re- composed family was re-referred with at least one child previously assigned to the intervention group and at least one child previously assigned to control, all children in such conflicting-status referrals were assigned to the intervention group. A small (N = 80) subset of children in the analysis sample therefore switched from control to intervention status during the trial. We check the robustness of our results to this complication in Table A.6. - The March 2021 correction introduced a second challenge: children without a listed biological mother were randomly assigned an intervention status at the individual level instead of at the sibling-group level. Given the concurrent change that assigned referrals with conflicting-status children to the intervention group, beginning in March 2021 larger sibling groups were more likely to be assigned to the intervention group. For example, a group of three siblings with- out a listed mother was assigned to control with a probability of: 1 2 · 1 2 · 1 2 = 1 8 instead of the intended 1 2. Reassuringly, four fifths of referrals had a mother listed and were not subject to this error. Furthermore, for the N = 843 children without a listed mother, treatment assignment remained random conditional on the number of listed children. We therefore include controls for each sibling group size greater than one for children listed without a mother and who were first randomized on or after March 2021. We refer to these controls throughout the paper as “randomization controls.” 2. Hospital Outcomes Sample. Although maltreatment likely increases the incidence of hospitaliza- tion, it may take several months for improvements in home environment to translate to changes in hospitalization. To minimize bias toward zero in treatment effects from not allowing sufficient time to measure hospitalization after randomization (which we had not thought about when pre-registering), we show results using hospital outcomes for those children randomized during the first year of the trial, which we call our “hospital outcomes sample” or “hospital sample” for short. Statewide linked hospital records are available through the end of June 2022, allowing us at least eight months of hos- pital records after randomization – or six months after a potential 60-day case opening period – for all children in the hospital sample (as opposed to only three months for the last children referred in our trial). This sample restriction was not pre-registered, but we show in Table A.6 that results are consistent if we use the full sample. 3. Aggregating Hospital Outcomes. Although our pre-analysis plan listed a set of key medical out- comes using hospital data, we had not pre-specified how we would aggregate effects across different outcomes. Acknowledging this, we report various ways one could aggregate results in Table A.6 and show that our results do not depend on how we aggregate our hospital outcome variables together. 76 4. Gender Disparities. We had pre-registered examining disparities by race, ethnicity, and socioeco- nomic status. However, given that we also find gender health disparities in our setting, and these disparities were of interest to the agency partner, we therefore also examine effects of the algorithm tool on gender health disparities. 77 Appendix D: Proofs The following propositions assume that the algorithm reduces noise in workers’ perception of child risk. name of paper: Scenario analysis with multivariate Bayesian machine learning models
summary: We present an econometric framework that adapts tools for scenario analysis, such as conditional forecasts and generalized impulse response functions, for use with dynamic nonparametric multivariate models. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through an exercise with simulated data, and three real-world applications: (i) scenario-based conditional forecasts aligned with Federal Reserve Bank stress test assumptions, (ii) measuring macroeconomic risk under varying financial conditions, and (iii) the asymmetric effects of US-based financial shocks and their international spillovers. Our results indicate the importance of nonlinearities and asymmetries in the dynamic relationship between macroeconomic and financial variables.
